group.name: Linux for Newbies
group.description: A beginner-friendly series that walks new users through core Linux concepts, from installation to your first shell script.

articles.title: What Is Linux and Why Should You Learn It?
articles.excerpt: A quick tour of what Linux actually is, where you'll find it running, and why it's worth learning even if you'll never touch a server.
articles.body:
## What Is Linux?

Linux is a free, open-source operating system kernel, first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Paired with GNU tools and a package manager, it forms a complete OS - usually called a **Linux distribution** (or *distro* for short), like Ubuntu, Debian, or Fedora.

## Where You'll Find It

- Most of the internet's servers and cloud infrastructure (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure)
- Android phones (built on the Linux kernel)
- Embedded devices: routers, smart TVs, cars
- A growing share of developer laptops and desktops

## Why Learn It

- **Free and open source** - no license fees, and you can inspect or modify anything.
- **Industry standard for servers** - if you're going into software, DevOps, or system administration, you'll use it constantly.
- **Powerful command line** - once you're comfortable with the terminal, many tasks become faster than clicking through a GUI.
- **Great for learning how computers actually work** - Linux doesn't hide as much from you as other operating systems do.

In the rest of this series we'll install a distro, learn to navigate the filesystem, run essential commands, manage permissions and packages, and write your first shell script.

articles.title: Installing Linux: Choosing Your First Distro
articles.excerpt: Overwhelmed by the hundreds of Linux distributions out there? Here's how to pick one and get it running - no risk to your current OS required.
articles.body:
## Picking a Distro

For a first distro, prioritize a large community and beginner-friendly defaults:

- **Ubuntu** - the most popular beginner distro, huge community, tons of tutorials.
- **Linux Mint** - Ubuntu-based, feels closer to a traditional desktop.
- **Fedora** - great if you want newer software and a taste of what Red Hat-based systems look like.

## Try It Without Installing Anything

You don't have to commit right away:

1. **Live USB** - download an ISO, flash it to a USB drive with a tool like Rufus or balenaEtcher, and boot from it. Nothing touches your hard drive unless you choose to install.
2. **Virtual machine** - install VirtualBox or VMware and run Linux inside a window on your current OS. Perfect for safe experimentation.
3. **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)** - if you're on Windows, `wsl --install` gets you a real Linux environment without leaving Windows.

## A Minimal Install Checklist

- Back up anything important first.
- Download the ISO and verify its checksum.
- Create bootable media (or just use a VM).
- Boot, follow the installer, pick a username/password you'll remember.
- Update the system immediately after first boot.

Once you're in, open a terminal - that's where the next lesson picks up.

articles.title: Navigating the Linux Filesystem
articles.excerpt: Everything in Linux is a file - here's the folder structure you'll actually need to know, and the commands to move around it.
articles.body:
## The Filesystem Tree

Linux organizes everything under a single root directory, `/`. There's no `C:\` - just one tree.

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/home/<user>` | Your personal files, like `C:\Users\<name>` |
| `/etc` | System-wide configuration files |
| `/var` | Logs, caches, and other variable data |
| `/bin`, `/usr/bin` | Executable programs |
| `/tmp` | Temporary files, cleared on reboot |
| `/root` | The root (admin) user's home directory |

## Core Navigation Commands

```bash
pwd          # print working directory - where am I?
ls           # list files in the current directory
ls -la       # list all files, including hidden ones, in long format
cd Documents # change into the Documents directory
cd ..        # go up one directory
cd ~         # jump straight to your home directory
cd -         # jump back to the previous directory
```

## Absolute vs Relative Paths

- **Absolute**: starts from `/`, e.g. `/home/minh/notes.txt` - always points to the same place.
- **Relative**: starts from where you currently are, e.g. `notes.txt` or `../notes.txt`.

## Useful Shortcuts

- `.` means the current directory
- `..` means the parent directory
- `~` means your home directory

Spend a few minutes just wandering around your filesystem with `ls` and `cd` - it's the fastest way to build a mental map of the system.

articles.title: Essential Linux Terminal Commands for Beginners
articles.excerpt: The dozen or so commands that cover almost everything you'll do in a terminal during your first month with Linux.
articles.body:
## File & Directory Basics

```bash
touch notes.txt        # create an empty file
mkdir projects         # create a directory
cp notes.txt backup.txt  # copy a file
mv backup.txt archive/   # move (or rename) a file
rm old-notes.txt       # delete a file
rm -r old-folder       # delete a directory and its contents
```

## Reading Files

```bash
cat notes.txt      # print the whole file
less notes.txt     # scroll through a file page by page (q to quit)
head -n 20 log.txt # first 20 lines
tail -n 20 log.txt # last 20 lines
tail -f log.txt    # follow a file live as it grows (great for logs)
```

## Finding Things

```bash
grep "error" log.txt        # search for a word inside a file
find . -name "*.txt"        # find files by name under the current directory
which python3               # show where a command is installed
```

## Processes

```bash
ps aux          # list running processes
top             # live view of process/CPU/memory usage
kill 1234       # stop the process with PID 1234
```

## Getting Help

```bash
man ls        # the manual page for a command
ls --help     # a quick usage summary
```

You won't memorize all of this at once - keep `man` and `--help` close and look things up as you go. That's normal, even for experienced users.

articles.title: Understanding File Permissions in Linux
articles.excerpt: Why is 'permission denied' the first error every Linux beginner hits? Here's what those rwx letters actually mean and how to fix it safely.
articles.body:
## Reading `ls -l` Output

```bash
$ ls -l notes.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 minh minh 128 Jan 20 10:00 notes.txt
```

The first column breaks down like this:

- Position 1: file type (`-` = regular file, `d` = directory, `l` = symlink)
- Positions 2-4: **owner** permissions (`rw-`)
- Positions 5-7: **group** permissions (`r--`)
- Positions 8-10: **everyone else** permissions (`r--`)

`r` = read, `w` = write, `x` = execute.

## Changing Permissions

```bash
chmod +x script.sh        # add execute permission for everyone
chmod 644 notes.txt       # owner: rw-, group: r--, others: r--
chmod 755 script.sh       # owner: rwx, group: r-x, others: r-x
```

The numeric mode adds up: read=4, write=2, execute=1. So `7` = 4+2+1 = `rwx`, and `5` = 4+1 = `r-x`.

## Changing Ownership

```bash
sudo chown minh:minh notes.txt   # set owner and group
```

## About `sudo`

`sudo` ("superuser do") temporarily runs a single command with administrator privileges. Use it deliberately - it's the difference between "this command might mess something up" and "this command WILL affect the whole system if I get it wrong."

```bash
sudo apt update   # run just this one command as admin
```

Avoid running an entire shell as `root` unless you have a specific reason - it's easy to make a permanent mistake.

articles.title: Installing and Managing Software with Package Managers
articles.excerpt: Forget hunting for .exe installers - Linux software comes from repositories managed by a package manager. Here's how that works.
articles.body:
## What Is a Package Manager?

Instead of downloading installers from random websites, Linux distros ship with a **package manager** that installs, updates, and removes software from trusted repositories - similar in spirit to an app store, but for the command line.

## Debian/Ubuntu: `apt`

```bash
sudo apt update             # refresh the list of available packages
sudo apt upgrade            # upgrade all installed packages
sudo apt install git        # install a package
sudo apt remove git         # remove a package
apt search text-editor      # search for a package
```

## Fedora/RHEL: `dnf`

```bash
sudo dnf check-update
sudo dnf install git
sudo dnf remove git
```

## Arch: `pacman`

```bash
sudo pacman -Syu            # sync and upgrade everything
sudo pacman -S git          # install a package
sudo pacman -R git          # remove a package
```

## Universal Formats

You'll also see cross-distro package formats:

- **Snap** - `sudo snap install code`
- **Flatpak** - `flatpak install flathub org.videolan.VLC`

These bundle their own dependencies, so they work the same way regardless of distro, at the cost of a larger download.

## Rule of Thumb

Prefer your distro's native package manager (`apt`/`dnf`/`pacman`) first - it integrates best with the system. Reach for Snap/Flatpak when software isn't available natively.

articles.title: Basic Linux Networking Commands
articles.excerpt: Check your IP, test connectivity, and diagnose network issues with a handful of commands every Linux user should know.
articles.body:
## Checking Your Network Configuration

```bash
ip addr show      # modern way to view network interfaces and IP addresses
ip route          # view the routing table / default gateway
hostname -I       # quick way to print your machine's IP address(es)
```

## Testing Connectivity

```bash
ping google.com          # check if a host is reachable (Ctrl+C to stop)
curl -I https://qminh.com  # fetch just the HTTP headers from a URL
wget https://example.com/file.zip  # download a file
```

## DNS Lookups

```bash
nslookup qminh.com
dig qminh.com
```

Both resolve a domain name to its IP address; `dig` gives more detail and is preferred by most sysadmins today.

## Checking Open Ports & Connections

```bash
ss -tulpn      # list listening ports and the processes using them
```

## SSH: Connecting to Remote Machines

```bash
ssh user@192.168.1.100        # connect to a remote server
scp file.txt user@host:/path  # copy a file to a remote server
```

These few commands cover diagnosing "why can't I reach this server" for the vast majority of everyday situations.

articles.title: Creating Your First Shell Script
articles.excerpt: Turn a sequence of terminal commands into a reusable script - the first real step from 'using Linux' to 'automating Linux'.
articles.body:
## Why Scripts?

Any sequence of commands you type more than twice is a candidate for a script. Shell scripts automate repetitive terminal work.

## Your First Script

Create a file called `greet.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# A minimal greeting script

echo "Hello, $(whoami)!"
echo "Today is $(date)"
echo "You're in: $(pwd)"
```

The `#!/bin/bash` on the first line is called a **shebang** - it tells the system which interpreter to run the script with.

## Making It Executable

```bash
chmod +x greet.sh   # grant execute permission
./greet.sh          # run it (the ./ is required unless it's on your PATH)
```

## Variables and Conditionals

```bash
#!/bin/bash

name="Minh"

if [ "$name" = "Minh" ]; then
  echo "Welcome back, $name."
else
  echo "Who are you, $name?"
fi
```

## A Practical Example: Backup Script

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Back up a directory with a timestamped filename

SOURCE="$HOME/projects"
DEST="$HOME/backups/projects-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tar.gz"

mkdir -p "$HOME/backups"
tar -czf "$DEST" "$SOURCE"
echo "Backed up $SOURCE to $DEST"
```

That's a real, useful script in eight lines. From here, the natural next steps are loops, functions, and scheduling scripts with `cron` - but even this much already saves you from retyping the same commands every day.
